query: Consider the following context: The recent perspective of multiprincipal element alloys (MPEAs), also known as high-entropy alloys (HEAs), has emerged as a very promising area for material design. Additive manufacturing (AM) strategies have also been noted to provide additional strength to HEA systems. In the selected dual-nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA system, an additional strength of approximately 300–400 MPa was achieved by adopting an additive manufacturing route as compared to its cast and wrought counterparts. However, the challenge of oxidation degradation always imposes a severe limitation for high-temperature applications in gas turbines, power plants, and aerospace components. Hence, ensuring material sustainability, longevity, and integrity for high-temperature applications inevitably requires the exploration of the oxidation behavior of alloys. In that context, which method can be used for elucidating the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates on oxidation behavior, and why?

generation.hypothesis: In situ high‐temperature X‐ray diffraction (HTXRD) can be employed to elucidate the mechanistic aspects and elemental redistribution of nanoprecipitates during oxidation in the dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy, because it provides real‐time phase identification and structural evolution tracking under controlled oxidation conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Dual‐nanoprecipitation Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high‐entropy alloy produced by an additive manufacturing route with well‐dispersed nanoprecipitates.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled high‐temperature oxidation environment while simultaneously collecting in situ XRD data.
generation.conditions: High temperature (e.g., 700–1100 °C) in a controlled atmosphere (air or oxygen partial pressure adjusted) to initiate oxidation.
generation.structural_mediator: The nanoprecipitates, which may act as preferential oxidation sites and influence the formation of protective or non‐protective oxide layers.
generation.mechanism: Oxidation induces phase transformations and elemental redistribution from the nanoprecipitates. HTXRD can capture transient oxide phases and shifts in lattice parameters that infer oxidation mechanisms and elemental migration.
generation.predicted_outcome: In situ XRD measurements will reveal the emergence and evolution of oxide phases, indicate shifts in lattice parameters, and correlate these changes with the redistribution of specific alloying elements from the nanoprecipitates, differing from the behavior observed in conventionally processed counterparts.
generation.baseline: Oxidation behavior characterized in cast or wrought variants of the alloy without the dual nanoprecipitation microstructure.
generation.boundary: Observations are limited to laboratory-scale high-temperature oxidation tests and the time-resolved phase transformations may not directly capture long-term oxidation effects in industrial applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of oxide formation, the threshold temperatures for significant elemental redistribution, and quantitative phase fraction changes require further empirical calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare samples of the dual‐nanoprecipitation HEA and subject them to in situ HTXRD during a high-temperature oxidation experiment. Compare the phase evolution, oxide scale formation, and lattice parameter changes with a control sample (cast/wrought counterpart) under identical oxidation conditions.
measurements: Real-time XRD patterns to detect emergent oxide phases
Lattice parameter shifts indicating elemental redistribution
Ex situ electron microscopy and EDS mapping for validation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if in situ HTXRD data does not show any discernible phase transformations or lattice shifts related to nanoprecipitate oxidation and elemental redistribution, or if the observed oxidation behavior of the AM-produced dual‐nanoprecipitation alloy is statistically indistinguishable from that of the cast/wrought counterpart under the same testing conditions.

Abstract The corrosion behavior of the FCC Cr 18 Mn 27 Fe 27.5 Ni 27.5 high entropy alloy (HEA) after exposure to molten FLiBe salt at 700 °C for 1000 hours, has been investigated. Results show that the HEA lost a higher mass compared to the reference 316 H stainless steel due to the dissolution of Mn into the molten salt. The loss of Mn from the alloy appeared to discourage the dissolution of Cr in the molten fluoride salts which is widely recognized as the mechanism of corrosion degradation. Thermal exposure at 700 °C for 1000 hours also led to the precipitation of an additional BCC phase Cr 67 Fe 13 Mn 18.5 Ni 1.5 , which was confirmed by CALPHAD predictions. Subject terms: Structural materials, Metals and alloys
